title: Menopause
intro: Menopause is the time when menstrual periods stop permanently, usually around the age of fifty. The years leading up to it, called perimenopause, bring hormonal changes that may cause hot flushes, sleep problems and mood changes. It is a natural stage of life, and many options exist for those who find symptoms difficult.

sections.heading: What happens in the body
paragraphs: The ovaries gradually produce less oestrogen and progesterone. Periods become irregular before ending. Menopause is confirmed after twelve months without a period. Perimenopause may last several years, and symptoms vary widely; some women have few, others many.

sections.heading: Common symptoms
paragraphs: Hot flushes and night sweats are the best-known symptoms. Others include sleep disturbance, mood changes, irritability, difficulty concentrating, joint aches, vaginal dryness, discomfort during sex, urinary symptoms and reduced libido. Heavy or very irregular bleeding, bleeding after menopause or bleeding between periods should be assessed by a doctor.

sections.heading: What you can do yourself
paragraphs: Regular exercise, a balanced diet, limiting alcohol and caffeine, stopping smoking and wearing layers can help. Cool bedrooms, relaxation techniques and cognitive behavioural therapy ease hot flushes and sleep problems. Vaginal moisturisers and lubricants relieve dryness.

sections.heading: Medical treatments
paragraphs: Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and also helps vaginal symptoms and protects bone. It carries risks that depend on the type, dose, duration and a woman's age and health, such as a slightly higher risk of blood clots and breast cancer with long-term use of some combinations. Local vaginal oestrogen is effective for vaginal symptoms with minimal absorption. Non-hormonal medicines may help hot flushes when hormones are unsuitable.

sections.heading: Long-term health
paragraphs: After menopause, bones lose density faster and the risk of heart disease increases. Weight-bearing exercise, enough calcium and vitamin D, avoiding smoking and checking blood pressure and cholesterol are sensible. Contraception is still needed for a period after the last period until menopause is confirmed.

examples.title: Preparing for a visit
examples.text: Imagine you wake at night soaked in sweat. You could keep a symptom diary for two weeks, list your questions about hormone therapy and your family history, and take it to your appointment.

examples.title: Discussing intimacy
examples.text: Suppose intercourse has become painful. You might ask your doctor about vaginal oestrogen and lubricants and discuss it with your partner.
